title: Invited to someone's home
goal: Be a good guest in an Egyptian home — and learn to read one custom that often trips up foreigners: offers you should decline, and refusals you should push back on.
bekal: accept and decline invitations with natural phrases
use the right phrases when arriving, eating, complimenting, and leaving
tell when an offer is really an offer

dialogs.title: حوار — على العشا في بيت منى
dialogs.intro: Budi arrives at Mona's family home with a box of pastries. Mona's mother opens the door.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.text: أهلاً وسهلاً! نورت البيت يا بودي.
lines.baca: ahlan wi sahlan! nawwart il-bēt ya Buudi.
lines.id: Welcome! You've lit up the house, Budi.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: البيت منور بأهله. ده حاجة بسيطة.
lines.baca: il-bēt minawwar bi-ahlu. da haaga basiiṭa.
lines.id: The house is already lit up by its family. This is just a little something.
lines.literal: the-house lit-up by-its-people. this thing simple.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.text: ما كنتش لازم تتعب نفسك! اتفضل اقعد.
lines.baca: ma kuntish laazim tit‘ab nafsak! itfaḍḍal u’‘ud.
lines.id: You shouldn't have gone to the trouble! Please, sit down.
lines.literal: not you-were must you-tire yourself! please sit.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Thank you. The house is really lovely.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.text: ده بيتك. تشرب إيه؟ شاي ولا عصير؟
lines.id: It's your home. What would you like to drink? Tea or juice?
lines.literal: this your-house. you-drink what? tea or juice?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Anything, please don't go to any trouble.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.text: تعب إيه! ده بيت أهلك. حاعملك شاي.
lines.baca: ta‘ab ’ēh! da bēt ahlak. ha‘millak shaay.
lines.id: What trouble! This is your family's home. I'll make you some tea.
lines.literal: tiredness what! this house your-family. I-will-make-you tea.

lines.speaker: منى:
lines.text: بابا حييجي بعد شوية. هو لسه في الشغل.
lines.baca: baaba hayiigi ba‘d shuwayya. huwwa lissa fish-shughl.
lines.id: Dad will be here in a bit. He's still at work.
lines.literal: dad he-will-come after a-little. he still at-the-work.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.id: Come on, Budi. The food is ready.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ما شاء الله! ده أكل يوم عيد.
lines.id: Mashallah! This is a feast-day meal.
lines.literal: what God-willed! this food day feast.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.id: Have some more. You haven't eaten a thing!

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: والله شبعت. الأكل تحفة، تسلم إيديكي.
lines.baca: wallaahi shib‘it. il-akl tuhfa, tislam idēki.
lines.id: Honestly, I'm full. The food is amazing, bless your hands.
lines.literal: by-God I-got-full. the-food masterpiece, be-safe your-two-hands.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.text: ولا حاجة. المرة الجاية تيجي بدري وتقعد أكتر.
lines.baca: wala haaga. il-marra g-gayya tiigi badri wi tu’‘ud aktar.
lines.id: It's nothing. Next time come earlier and stay longer.
lines.literal: nor thing. the-time the-coming you-come early and you-stay more.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: إن شاء الله. أنا اتشرفت أوي.
lines.id: God willing. It's been a real honor.
lines.literal: if God willed. I I-was-honored very.

lines.speaker: أم منى:
lines.text: البيت بيتك، تعالى في أي وقت. مع السلامة.
lines.baca: il-bēt bētak, ta‘aala fi ayyi wa’t. ma‘a s-salaama.
lines.id: Our home is your home, come any time. Goodbye.
lines.literal: the-house your-house, come in any time. with the-safety.

notes: **The word نورت and its reply البيت منور بأهله are a pair that should never be split.** The host says "you've lit up (the house)", and the guest replies "the house is already lit up by its family". Accepting the compliment without turning it back feels a little graceless.
**The phrase ما كنتش لازم is the standard way to receive a gift**, literally "you didn't have to". The right reply is to play down your own gift: ده حاجة بسيطة (it's just a little thing).

**The phrase تعب نفسك literally means "tire yourself", and it is how Egyptians say "go to trouble".** You'll say the negative ماتتعبش نفسك every time your host gets up to fetch something — and every time it will be cheerfully ignored.

**Turning down more food just once won't be accepted.** An Egyptian host will keep filling your plate until you say it clearly, with an oath: والله شبعت. Here والله is not a religious oath but an intensifier — without it, your refusal is read as mere politeness.
**The phrase تسلم إيديكي uses the form for two hands.** To a man تسلم إيدك, to a woman تسلم إيديكي — and the second is warmer, since cooking takes both hands. The reply is وإيديك.

**The phrase البيت بيتك is not empty politeness.** In Egypt, a guest who has been inside a home is seen as having the right to come back without a fresh invitation, and staying away too long can actually read as distance.

grammars.title: Invitations: offering, accepting, declining
body: Egyptian has set phrases for every stage, and using them matters far more than building your own sentences.

head: Stage
مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: would you like to have dinner with us?
I'd love for you to come
let me check and get back to you
sorry, I have a prior engagement

after: Declining an invitation in Egypt almost always needs **a reason and a promise for next time**. A bare لأ، شكراً sounds like you're rejecting the person, not the event.
The phrase أشوف وأرد عليك is a polite middle way when you can't decide yet. It is understood as a real maybe, not a soft no.
The word متشكر means "thankful" and is an active participle: متشكر، متشكرة، متشكرين. It is warmer than the lighter شكراً.

grammars.title: Offers you have to read twice
body: This is what most often trips up foreigners in Egypt: some offers are real, and some are just good manners.

head: Situation
What's said
What it really means
rows: You're eating and someone walks by
a real offer, OK to decline
not yet taken as a no

after: A rule of thumb that rarely fails: **an offer from someone who invited you is real; an offer from someone who didn't is politeness.** Your host truly wants you to eat; a street vendor who says خد ببلاش does not.
The phrase قابل نداره literally means "it's worth nothing", and shopkeepers say it when you go to pay. It's custom, not a gift. The reply: لأ، لازم، تفضل — and then pay.

blocks.text: Notice that almost every reply uses الله or ربنا. This is not a sign of special piety but part of the fabric of the language — Coptic Christians use exactly the same phrases. Avoiding them would only make you sound stiff.

blocks.title: What to bring when you visit
items: Usual choices: cakes from a pastry shop (جاتوه *gatōh*), fruit, chocolate, or baklava. Flowers are less common, except for someone who is ill.
Best avoided if you don't know the family well: alcohol, and gifts that are too expensive — the latter can make your host feel indebted.
Don't open the box yourself, and don't be surprised if your host just sets it aside without opening it in front of you. Opening a gift in front of the giver isn't usual in Egypt.

blocks.text: These phrases follow the order of a visit, from knocking on the door to saying goodbye.

head: مصري
Say it
Meaning
rows: should I take my shoes off?
please don't go to any trouble

blocks.text: The phrase أستأذن بقى is a gentle way to take your leave, literally "I ask permission". It gives your host the chance to hold you back once — which they almost certainly will, saying بدري أوي! After the second refusal, your goodbye is accepted.

vocab.en: welcome (lit. you've lit up the place)

exercises.prompt: Write the right reply to each phrase.
Write the right phrase for each situation.
items: You walk into someone's home and compliment it.
Your host gets up to make tea and you want to stop them.
Your host refills your plate, but you're already full.
You want to compliment the cooking.
You want to take your leave politely.
This is just a little something.
Please don't go to any trouble.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.

answers: البيت منور بأهله. — الله يهنيك. — وإيديك. — الله يبارك فيك. — وانت طيب.
البيت جميل أوي. — ماتتعبيش نفسك. — والله شبعت، الأكل تحفة. — تسلم إيديكي. — أستأذن بقى.
ده حاجة بسيطة. — ماتتعبش نفسك. — الأكل تحفة. — والله شبعت. — أنا اتشرفت أوي.
نورت البيت يا بودي. — البيت منور بأهله. — ده حاجة بسيطة. — ماتتعبيش نفسك. — والله شبعت.
wave: Tonight, imagine you've been invited to dinner and say out loud the ten phrases you'd use — from the front door to goodbye.
